  <entry>
    <id>tag:appaddict.app,2005:Post/17818</id>
    <published>2026-04-29T01:29:37Z</published>
    <updated>2026-04-29T01:29:38Z</updated>
    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/tolaria-a-files-first-markdown-app-for-mac-designed-for-git-workflows-and-ai-agents"/>
    <title>Tolaria: a files-first Markdown app for Mac designed for Git workflows and AI agents</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--png"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" alt="Tolaria" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBeUtpQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--2110fe116496acd97df7bf106cc5b4fc909dad62/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJY0c1bkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUNHa0NBQVk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2Q25OMGNtbHdWRG9NY1hWaGJHbDBlV2xrIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--768aeab7fb7843d85fe5b2b4ba237e06e6ef604f/tolaria-full-layout.png" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
    &lt;figcaption class="attachment__caption text-center"&gt;
      Tolaria
    &lt;/figcaption&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://tolaria.md"&gt;Tolaria&lt;/a&gt; is a free, open-source desktop app for macOS and Linux built by Luca Rossi, the author of the &lt;i&gt;&lt;em&gt;Refactoring&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/i&gt; newsletter. Rossi created Tolaria to manage his own collection of 10,000+ notes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That origin story matters. The feature set feels like it grew out of solving real problems for a real workflow; not something assembled by a product manager or stitched together from an AI roadmap.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;At its core, Tolaria is a very 2026-style Markdown editor; modern, opinionated, and not trying to clone Notion or compete head-on with Obsidian.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The sweet-spot user is someone who:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Already lives in Markdown and Git&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Is experimenting with tools like Claude Code or other AI agents in their daily workflow&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Wants their knowledge base to be part of their AI context instead of isolated from it&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Treats data portability as a non-negotiable requirement&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Tolaria’s Core Principles&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;These are deliberate design choices from the developer.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Files-first.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Notes are plain &lt;code&gt;.md&lt;/code&gt; files on disk. No proprietary database; no export step. Open them in BBEdit, Obsidian, Vim, or anything else that understands Markdown.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Git-first.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Every vault is a Git repository. You get full version history and can push to any remote you like. There are no Tolaria servers; the app doesn’t depend on one.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That alone sets it apart from a lot of the field.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Offline-first, zero lock-in.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;No account. No subscription. The vault works completely offline.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Open source (AGPL-3.0).&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;The code lives on GitHub. You can read it, fork it, and run your own build if you want.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What It’s Not&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tolaria is not trying to be Notion.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There’s no relational database layer, no property-driven schemas, and no team collaboration platform. That trade-off is intentional; those features usually come with heavier infrastructure and less portability.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It also doesn’t have anything close to Obsidian’s plugin ecosystem. If your workflow depends on dozens of community plugins, Tolaria probably isn’t ready to replace Obsidian yet. It’s a younger, more focused tool.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Another practical detail: it runs on Mac and Linux only; there’s no Windows version. For some people that’s a dealbreaker. For others, it’s perfectly fine.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;AI Support and Integration&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is where Tolaria earns its “second brain for the AI era” tagline.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Instead of bolting on a chat sidebar, the app treats your knowledge vault as something AI agents can actually work with.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tolaria includes built-in support for tools like Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI. It automatically generates a shared &lt;code&gt;AGENTS.md&lt;/code&gt; file in the vault root. That file explains the structure and conventions of your notes, and every supported AI tool reads the same one.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The practical benefit: you maintain a single source of truth for how your vault is organized instead of writing separate instructions for each model you’re experimenting with.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tolaria also runs a local MCP (Model Context Protocol) server. When you connect an external AI tool, your vault is registered as a structured context source that the agent can query directly.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Most “AI-enabled” note apps just add a chat window. Tolaria takes a different approach: it lets AI agents navigate and operate on the vault itself using standard protocols.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There are also vault-level permission modes, so agents don’t automatically get full write access to your notes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Power-User Bonus Feature&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tolaria clearly targets people who prefer keyboards over mice.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The Command Palette is central to the workflow, and the editor is designed around keyboard navigation. If you spend time in tools like Raycast, Keyboard Maestro, or VS Code, the design philosophy will feel familiar.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is the difference between a command palette that drives the interface and one that feels bolted on as an afterthought.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Availability and Pricing&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tolaria is free and open source.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can download it from &lt;a href="https://tolaria.md"&gt;tolaria.md&lt;/a&gt; or build it yourself from the GitHub repository.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;No subscription. No account. No catch.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Hat tip to &lt;a href="https://labnotes.org/weekend-reading-dream-of-bigger-things/?ref=labnotes-by-assaf-arkin-newsletter"&gt;Labnotes&lt;/a&gt; for once again, being the first to write about a new tool&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Tolaria:%20a%20files-first%20Markdown%20app%20for%20Mac%20designed%20for%20Git%20workflows%20and%20AI%20agents" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>

  <entry>
    <id>tag:appaddict.app,2005:Post/16235</id>
    <published>2026-04-21T17:06:17Z</published>
    <updated>2026-04-21T17:06:19Z</updated>
    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/dockside-turns-drag-and-drop-into-a-real-workflow"/>
    <title>Dockside Turns Drag-And-Drop Into a Real Workflow</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" alt="Dockside" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBenlUQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--c477ea28ee5cd6418e099737d9ba46f38cb5c80c/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUNHa0NBQVk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2Q25OMGNtbHdWRG9NY1hWaGJHbDBlV2xrIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--daf4078a1aefa3c961be2c7b8fbe4a74a2641c0c/CleanShot%202026-04-21%20at%2013.04.19.jpg" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
    &lt;figcaption class="attachment__caption text-center"&gt;
      Dockside
    &lt;/figcaption&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Most Mac users already rely on drag-and-drop constantly, but macOS never really gave us a good place to &lt;i&gt;&lt;em&gt;stage&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/i&gt; things temporarily. Finder windows work, but they’re clumsy for quick hand-offs between apps.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dockside turns that gap into a system. It acts like a permanent drop zone beside your Dock where you can park files, preview them, batch them, trigger actions, and move them between apps without juggling Finder windows.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Turning Drag and Drop Into a System&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Just because you want to use a file shelf utility doesn’t mean you should have to manage yet another window cluttering your workspace.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Shelf location is a feature; an important one. With Dockside, the shelf lives beside your Dock or on any edge of your display you choose. It’s always where your muscle memory expects it. It’s definitely not another window you have to manage.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dockside’s strength isn’t just acting as a landing strip for files. It includes multiple purpose-built shelf areas, a secondary space for screenshots, downloads, recents, and clipboard history, plus stacks, Quick Look, utilities, and; this is where the real power lives; drop zones that can trigger Shortcuts, scripts, or file actions based on what you drop.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;What Dockside Is and Isn’t&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dockside is a native-feeling macOS file shelf and Dock companion. You drag in files, folders, apps, images, video, links, or text; park them temporarily; preview or batch-select them; then drag them out to Finder or into apps.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It’s &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;not&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; a “Dock replacement.” It’s more like a workflow lane; close enough to the Dock to feel like it belongs to the OS, but customizable enough to act like a small command center.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Multi-Shelf Layout&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dockside gives each side of your Dock a different purpose.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Files shelf&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;The primary area where you drag files, folders, apps, images, video, links, or text.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Secondary shelf&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;By default this displays screenshots and downloads, but it can be configured to show several other categories:&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Recent files&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; (with exclusions and limits)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Clipboard history&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; (with capture toggles, exclusions, and regex rules)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Media controls&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; (Spotify or Apple Music)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;System info&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; (CPU, memory, disk, network, battery, uptime, temperatures)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Dragging; Opinionated in a Good Way&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dragging items out of Dockside is sophisticated in a way that shows how much thought went into its design.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Smart drag activation:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; open when dragging starts, when the cursor nears the shelf, or when it approaches the cursor; user choice.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Adjustable sensitivity:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; tune the delay and drop-zone height so it feels fast without triggering accidentally.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Store by alias or copy:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; keep lightweight aliases or store real copies inside Dockside.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Remove items after drag-out:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; great for true hand-off workflows.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The attention to detail is clear in the modifier-key behavior while dragging. You can remove items on drag-out with &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Option&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;, use Finder-style move vs copy behavior, ignore activation with &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Fn&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;, and more.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It’s the kind of app that gets noticeably better once your muscle memory kicks in.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;So Many Features&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I’ve been using Dockside for over a year. During that time the feature set has grown quite a bit without drifting into feature bloat.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Project Scratchpad&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can create and manage up to three separately configurable work zones in Dockside (for example: working copies, archive, future projects), each with its own automation rules based on tag filters or watched folders.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Clutter isn’t much of a problem because Dockside includes a &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;stack interface&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; and lets you create folders directly from selected files.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Drop Zones&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can configure multiple drop zones that appear when you drag items. Each zone has a user-definable primary action (Shortcut, Email, Copy or Move, AppleScript, shell script, CLI command, utilities, or none) and a post-drop action (keep in shelf, move or copy elsewhere, trash, or permanently delete).&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Utility Suite&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dockside includes a set of file utilities available from menus, hover actions, or assignable drop zones:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Compression and extraction&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Image to PDF&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Image metadata removal&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Rename&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Move or copy to predefined folders&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;ShareSheet&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Cloud uploads&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Clop integration for file size optimization&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Finder integration via a Finder Sync extension&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;What Makes Dockside Stand Out&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The problem with many apps in this category is inconsistent behavior. Elements move around unexpectedly, or panels hide and unhide randomly.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dockside has been rock solid in my experience.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can configure which display it appears on and which edge it attaches to. You choose how it hides or shows itself, either through settings or a global shortcut. Once configured, it behaves predictably. It just works.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It’s 100% a &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Mac-ass Mac app&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;. Standard keyboard shortcuts work as expected: ⌘C, ⌘V, ⌘A, ⌘⌫, and ⌘Z to restore. Multi-item selection is built in. There are trackpad and mouse gestures for expanding shelves and paginating items. The right-click context menu is practical and thoughtfully designed.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dockside is also Terminal friendly. It supports Apple Shortcuts and custom URLs. Not only does it work with Clop, it also includes a PopClip extension and sharing via Dropshare.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is a power user’s kind of utility. The developer is friendly and responsive, and the app fits into your workflow without forcing you to change how you work. It’s particularly well suited to juggling multiple projects at once. There’s also a two-week free trial, which is plenty of time to see whether it fits your workflow.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Real-World Uses&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;After a few weeks of using Dockside, certain workflows start to feel natural.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Temporary file staging&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Drag files from Finder, Mail, or Safari into Dockside while collecting materials for something. Once everything is there, drag them out together into the destination app.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Screenshot triage&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Screenshots land in the secondary shelf automatically. From there you can preview them with Quick Look, drop them into an image tool, or send them directly to a drop zone action.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Automation trigger pad&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Drop a file onto a zone that runs a Shortcut or shell script; resize images, move files to project folders, or trigger upload workflows.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Multi-project juggling&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Use separate scratchpad zones for active work, reference material, and future tasks without scattering Finder windows everywhere.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;The Details&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Activation on up to three Macs&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Apple notarized&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Privacy policy: no data collection; internet used mainly for license activation and checks&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Homebrew install supported (&lt;code&gt;brew install --cask dockside&lt;/code&gt;)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Cost: $5.99 lifetime; no subscription. I could easily see paying five times that for something this useful.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Developer website:&lt;br&gt;&lt;a href="https://hachipoo.com/dockside-app"&gt;Dockside for Mac — native file shelf &amp;amp; Dock companion (drag, drop, done)&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;The Verdict&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dockside is one of those tools that feels small at first and then quietly becomes part of your daily workflow.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you move files between apps constantly, collect materials for projects, or run file-based automations, it’s an easy recommendation. It behaves like a natural extension of macOS rather than another utility window competing for your attention.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Dockside%20Turns%20Drag-And-Drop%20Into%20a%20Real%20Workflow" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>
    <summary>Most Mac users already rely on drag-and-drop constantly, but macOS never really gave us a good place to stage things temporarily. Finder windows work, but they’re clumsy for quick hand-offs between apps.

Dockside turns that gap into a system. It acts like a permanent drop zone beside your Dock where...</summary>

    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/seeking-feedback-from-mac-power-users"/>
    <title>Seeking Feedback from Mac Power Users</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" alt="Mac Apps" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBL2FSQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--ae14ba59cae8a4ea4e75269c3ce974d8a063fe17/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUNHa0NBQVk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2Q25OMGNtbHdWRG9NY1hWaGJHbDBlV2xrIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--daf4078a1aefa3c961be2c7b8fbe4a74a2641c0c/CleanShot%202026-04-16%20at%2011.36.42.jpg" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
    &lt;figcaption class="attachment__caption text-center"&gt;
      Mac Apps
    &lt;/figcaption&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I’m looking for feedback on a few apps.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I’m looking for the answers to the following questions:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Did this app solve a problem you had? If so, what was the issue and the solution.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Who do you think is the target audience for the app&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;What’s your favorite feature or biggest aggravation with the app?&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://getbookshelves.app/"&gt;BookShelves eBook Reader -&lt;/a&gt; BookShelves is a modern ebook reader and library manager for macOS and iOS. It supports EPUB, PDF, MOBI, PRC, and Kindle formats with iCloud sync, a customizable reading experience, and thousands of free classic books built in.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://sidebarapp.net/"&gt;Sidebar -&lt;/a&gt; Sidebar is a MacOS application that replaces the standard MacOS Dock. It feels more like the taskbar of other operating systems (e.g. Windows, Linux).&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.vaultsort.com/"&gt;VaultSort - Organize, Secure, and Optimize Your Mac Files -&lt;/a&gt; File automation, cleanup, and security&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://pacificcoast.dev/#procman"&gt;Procman -&lt;/a&gt; Procman is a native process explorer for Mac that combines the hierarchy of pstree with the clarity of Activity Monitor. Instead of a flat list of processes, it shows a live parent-child tree so you can actually understand what spawned what, what’s consuming resources, and how everything fits together.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.liqoria.com/"&gt;Liqoria - Mac Music Player • Apple Music • Spotify • YouTube and more -&lt;/a&gt; An Apple Music alternative, improving your Spotify for Mac workflow, or comparing tools like Cider for Mac.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you have feedback, you can use the comment for here, send me an email or hit me up on Reddit, Mastodon or BlueSky.&lt;/p&gt;

    <id>tag:appaddict.app,2005:Post/16115</id>
    <published>2026-04-14T01:06:50Z</published>
    <updated>2026-04-14T01:29:10Z</updated>
    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/learning-and-using-github-as-a-non-developer-with-tower"/>
    <title>Learning and Using GitHub As a Non-Developer with Tower</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" alt="Tower" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBKzJRQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--a1f50152e6731aaff8f371c23c43bdbb8fccfeb3/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUNHa0NBQVk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2Q25OMGNtbHdWRG9NY1hWaGJHbDBlV2xrIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--daf4078a1aefa3c961be2c7b8fbe4a74a2641c0c/CleanShot%202026-04-13%20at%2021.02.32.jpg" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
    &lt;figcaption class="attachment__caption text-center"&gt;
      Tower
    &lt;/figcaption&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For years I assumed GitHub was only useful if you were a developer.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Turns out it's actually one of the best tools I've found for managing &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;text-heavy Mac workflows&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I now use Git repositories to version and back up things like:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;my 13K-file Obsidian vault (private)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;~700 Keyboard Maestro macros (public)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Hazel and BetterTouchTool configs (public)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;writing projects and scripts (private)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;~500 Markdown documents with my quotes collection (public)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;No coding required.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I recently switched from GitHub Desktop to &lt;a href="https://www.git-tower.com"&gt;Tower&lt;/a&gt;, which exposes a lot more of Git's capabilities without forcing you into the command line.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you're a Mac power user managing large folders of Markdown, scripts, or automation configs, Git is basically &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Time Machine for specific folders&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; — and Tower makes it easy to use.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why This Matters for Mac Power Users&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you work with text-heavy workflows on macOS — Markdown notes, scripts, automation configs, or documentation — Git gives you something Time Machine doesn’t:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;• version history for individual files&lt;br&gt;• the ability to roll back one specific edit&lt;br&gt;• an off-site backup of critical working folders&lt;br&gt;• synchronization between multiple Macs&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For people managing large Obsidian vaults, automation libraries, or documentation projects, that combination becomes extremely useful.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Let's Speak the Same Language&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Here's a quick translation of common Git terminology:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Repository&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A folder tracked by Git that contains files and their complete change history.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Commit&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A saved snapshot of the repository at a specific moment, along with a message describing the change.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;History&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The chronological record of all commits.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Branch&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A parallel line of development that lets you experiment without affecting the main version.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Merge&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Combining changes from one branch into another.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Remote&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A copy of the repository stored somewhere else; typically GitHub.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Push&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Send your local commits to the remote repository.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Pull&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Fetch changes from the remote repository and integrate them into your local copy.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Clone&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Download a complete copy of a repository, including its history.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Diff&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A comparison showing exactly what changed between two versions of a file.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Why I Use Tower&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tower provides a graphical interface for Git repositories and remote services such as GitHub. Instead of memorizing commands, you interact with commits, branches, and history visually.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For developers this manages source code. For everyone else it manages &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;collections of important files&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Git tracks the complete history of a folder. Every time you make a commit, Git records a snapshot of the repository. Tower simply exposes that system visually. Instead of typing commands like:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;pre data-language="plain"&gt;git add &lt;br&gt;git commit &lt;br&gt;git push&lt;/pre&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tower gives you:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;• checkboxes to stage files&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;• a commit message box&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;• push / pull buttons&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;• a visual timeline of changes&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The idea is so simple it's easy to miss how powerful it is.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Every commit becomes a permanent historical snapshot.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For writers, note-takers, and automation nerds, Git effectively becomes &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Time Machine for specific folders&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;; but with far more precision. Instead of restoring an entire folder, you can restore a &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;single edit inside a single file&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;. That capability becomes extremely valuable once your knowledge base grows large.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;I regularly use Tower to manage:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Markdown notes&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;scripts&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;documentation&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;configuration files&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;knowledge bases&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;writing projects

&lt;br&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Using Tower with GitHub adds a few major benefits:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;
&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;complete version history&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;off-site backup&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;synchronization between machines&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;detailed change tracking&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Tower Features Worth Highlighting&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Rebase&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tower includes a visual interface for &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;rebasing&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;, which allows you to reorganize commit history. The GUI makes operations that are intimidating on the command line much easier:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;reordering commits&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;editing commit messages&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;combining commits&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Stashing&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Suppose you're halfway through editing files but need to switch branches. You don't want to commit unfinished work. &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Stashing&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; temporarily saves those changes so you can switch contexts and return later.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Conflict Resolution&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I'll admit I tend to use more computers than I should. That occasionally creates conflicts. When multiple versions of a file diverge, Git produces a &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;merge conflict&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;. Tower provides a visual interface for resolving these conflicts instead of forcing you to edit raw conflict markers. For non-developers, this feature alone removes a lot of confusion.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Getting Started in Five Minutes&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can realistically start using Tower on macOS in about five minutes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Create a repository&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Pick a folder; your Obsidian vault is a good candidate. Initialize it as a Git repository in Tower.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;**Make the first commit&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tower will show all files in the folder. Select them and create the first commit.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Connect to GitHub&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Create a repository on GitHub and link it to your local repository. Push the files.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Adopt a simple daily workflow&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Open Tower; review the files that changed; write a short commit message; push to GitHub.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That's really all most non-developers need.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Details&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Tower Website&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.git-tower.com"&gt;https://www.git-tower.com&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Privacy Policy&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.git-tower.com/legal/privacy-policy"&gt;https://www.git-tower.com/legal/privacy-policy&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Price&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;$5.75/month billed annually&lt;/p&gt;

  <entry>
    <id>tag:appaddict.app,2005:Post/16047</id>
    <published>2026-04-11T01:25:20Z</published>
    <updated>2026-04-11T01:25:21Z</updated>
    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/three-creative-and-original-new-apps"/>
    <title>Three Creative and Original New Apps</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;h1&gt;&lt;br&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Developers keep finding interesting ways to make our existing tech more useful. Sometimes that means refining how we interact with tools we already rely on. Other times it means applying software to problems that don’t obviously look like “tech problems.”&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Here are three apps that take a slightly unconventional approach.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;a href="https://xspeak.app/"&gt;Xspeak&lt;/a&gt; — a meeting companion for people who sometimes struggle to articulate their thoughts in fast-moving conversations. It transcribes discussion in real time and helps you decide how and when to respond.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/drooid-news-from-all-sides/id6593684010"&gt;Drooid&lt;/a&gt; — a news reader that focuses on surfacing bias and showing how different outlets frame the same story.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;a href="https://parall.app/"&gt;Parall&lt;/a&gt; — a utility that lets you run multiple configurations of the same app simultaneously on a single Mac.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--webp"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBd21RQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--f7b010e7da2acdff95257cd9de1e4871d7281c20/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBPZ2h3Ym1jNkZISmxjMmw2WlY5MGIxOXNhVzFwZEZzSGFRSUFDR2tDQUFZNkNuTmhkbVZ5ZXdjNkNuTjBjbWx3VkRvTWNYVmhiR2wwZVdsayIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoidmFyaWF0aW9uIn19--63d820beee6b8696af3b0f76fc64159e37e92615/10.webp" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;XSpeak&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;What problem this solves&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; - Contributing effectively in meetings when conversations move faster than your ability to respond.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Xspeak is not a generic Whisper front end. It supports multiple on-device speech recognition models, and the entire design emphasizes privacy. If you prefer, you can also connect it to OpenAI-compatible cloud models.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The interesting part is what happens after transcription. XSpeak produces diarized transcripts and identifies questions that may require a response. With some setup and training, its on-device AI can suggest responses and strategies in real time during a meeting.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The system improves over time. Once you identify a speaker, XSpeak can recognize that voice in future meetings and remember their role in the conversation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;By default, it stores past meetings locally so you can reference them later. The app can generate summaries, insights, and suggested follow-ups. During a live meeting it also allows custom queries to the AI for additional context or analysis.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Highlights&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Diarized transcription&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Multiple local speech models&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Optional OpenAI-compatible cloud models&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Real-time suggestions during meetings&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Meeting summaries and follow-up analysis&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Local storage of past meetings&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Developer Website&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;&lt;a href="https://xspeak.app/"&gt;https://xspeak.app&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Privacy Policy&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;No data collection; processing and storage can remain fully on-device.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Pricing&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;$3.99/mo · $19.99/year · $49 lifetime&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Drooid&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBd3FRQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--1677857cf8cc83ecf6e884017878edcf746f5854/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUNHa0NBQVk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2Q25OMGNtbHdWRG9NY1hWaGJHbDBlV2xrIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--daf4078a1aefa3c961be2c7b8fbe4a74a2641c0c/CleanShot%202026-04-10%20at%2021.23.14.jpg" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;What problem this solves:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; Quickly comparing how different news outlets frame the same story.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I’ve followed news closely since I was a kid. Over the last decade, the media landscape has shifted in ways that make it harder to quickly evaluate what’s reliable and what’s not.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Drooid tries to address that problem by presenting the same story through multiple outlets and highlighting differences in framing and bias.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I initially assumed it would take a simplistic “both sides are the same” approach. That’s not what it does. Instead, it analyzes historical editorial patterns and presents coverage alongside contextual explanations of each source’s tendencies.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It’s also a capable news reader. You can follow topics, read summaries, jump to original reporting, and save stories for later.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;How Drooid Works&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Aggregates articles from established publishers&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Uses AI to generate structured summaries from multiple sources&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Identifies differences in perspective and framing&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Adds historical context and citations when relevant&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Provides deeper analysis for major stories&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;What You Can Do&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Read concise multi-source summaries&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Compare coverage across outlets&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Open original articles&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Explore deeper AI analysis&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Follow topics and people&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Search stories and events&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Participate in community discussion&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Save stories for later&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Drooid runs on Mac, iPhone, and iPad.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Instead of relying on a social media algorithm to decide what you see, Drooid gives you a structured way to compare coverage directly.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Developer Website&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;&lt;a href="https://drooid.social/"&gt;https://drooid.social&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Privacy Policy&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Collects some data but does not link it to your identity.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Pricing&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;$3.99/mo · $29.99/year&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Parall&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBd3VRQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--a205abf88347b7992acf1eaa6040149e3abf5789/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUNHa0NBQVk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2Q25OMGNtbHdWRG9NY1hWaGJHbDBlV2xrIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--daf4078a1aefa3c961be2c7b8fbe4a74a2641c0c/CleanShot%202026-04-10%20at%2021.24.39.jpg" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;What problem this solves:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; Running multiple independent instances of the same app without separate macOS accounts.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For years I used separate macOS accounts when I needed to run the same app with different configurations. Parall removes that requirement.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It creates configurable shortcuts that launch separate instances of supported apps, each with its own configuration and data environment.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Parall already supports many common third-party apps and can download compatibility profiles for apps it hasn’t explicitly tested yet. That approach lets the ecosystem expand without waiting for a full app update.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The original application isn’t modified. Parall simply launches isolated instances with different parameters. If you stop using the shortcuts, the original app behaves exactly as it always did.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Key Features&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Configurable launch shortcuts&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Separate configuration and data environments&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Custom launch arguments&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Visual indicators to distinguish instances&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Logging and debugging tools&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There are limits. Some apps cannot be isolated this way. Also, macOS security prompts appear frequently during setup, so expect to click through quite a few dialogs.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is not a beginner utility. If you are comfortable with launch arguments and environment variables, it makes immediate sense. If not, you can still use it; the learning curve is just a bit steeper.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Parall is one of those niche utilities that becomes surprisingly useful once you start using it. Separate Dock icons for different contexts; clean separation between work and personal accounts; isolated project environments; all without duplicate installs or brittle automation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Developer Website&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;&lt;a href="https://parall.app/"&gt;https://parall.app&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Privacy Policy&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Fully sandboxed macOS app. Operates locally by default and does not send network requests or collect personal data.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Price&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;$9.99 on the Mac App Store&lt;br&gt;&lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/parall/id6754065114?mt=12"&gt;https://apps.apple.com/us/app/parall/id6754065114?mt=12&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Who These Apps Are For&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;These are not generic productivity apps. Each one targets a specific workflow:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Xspeak&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; — people who participate in a lot of meetings and want real-time assistance organizing their thoughts.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Drooid&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; — readers who want structured comparisons of how news outlets frame the same story.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Parall&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; — power users who need multiple app environments without juggling macOS accounts or duplicate installs.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;None of these tools will appeal to everyone. But if the specific problem they solve matches your workflow, they are unusually thoughtful implementations.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Three%20Creative%20and%20Original%20New%20Apps" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>
    <summary>

Developers keep finding interesting ways to make our existing tech more useful. Sometimes that means refining how we interact with tools we already rely on. Other times it means applying software to problems that don’t obviously look like “tech problems.”

Here are three apps that take a slightly unconventional...</summary>

    <author>
      <name>Lou Plummer</name>
      <uri>https://appaddict.app</uri>
    </author>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>tag:appaddict.app,2005:Post/15998</id>
    <published>2026-04-09T01:32:06Z</published>
    <updated>2026-04-09T01:32:08Z</updated>
    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/organizing-a-660-app-applications-folder-with-apptela"/>
    <title>Organizing a 660-App /Applications Folder with AppTela</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" alt="AppTela" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBMXlQQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--74c8df767b0059a8cbc0320b2b049a44d6784a1c/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUNHa0NBQVk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2Q25OMGNtbHdWRG9NY1hWaGJHbDBlV2xrIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--daf4078a1aefa3c961be2c7b8fbe4a74a2641c0c/CleanShot%202026-04-08%20at%2021.28.30.jpg" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
    &lt;figcaption class="attachment__caption text-center"&gt;
      AppTela
    &lt;/figcaption&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I recently organized my &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;/Applications&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; folder; it contains more than &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;660 apps&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;. The tool that finally made it manageable is &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/apptela-app-launcher/id6752568197?mt=12"&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;AppTela&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/a&gt;, a layered, categorized launcher available for &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;$4.99 on the Mac App Store&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I tend to keep an app for every contingency. The problem isn’t disk space; it’s remembering the name of the utility you installed last year to solve a problem that only shows up every few months.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you’ve ever had the experience of knowing you &lt;i&gt;&lt;em&gt;have&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/i&gt; an app for something but not remembering what it’s called, AppTela is designed to solve exactly that problem. I still launch the majority of my apps from Raycast. My use case for AppTela is using it's organizational structure, but if you're primarily a mouse or trackpad (nothing wrong with that), then this app will server you well on that front.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Not many days go by without me downloading at least one app. I’ve been doing that for years. Some people golf; some people play video games. My hobby is testing software.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Over time, of course, some maintenance and culling becomes necessary. But I’ve never worried about having too many apps; if that’s even a thing. As long as I stay away from the big bundles from companies like Adobe and Microsoft and keep Electron apps to a minimum, disk space isn’t an issue. Even on a &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Mac mini with a 256 GB SSD&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;, my very full Applications folder uses &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;less than 20% of the drive&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;AppTela is &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;not&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; a Launchpad clone. It’s completely &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;non-destructive&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;. No matter how you organize things inside AppTela, your underlying file system never changes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The structure takes a little time to understand, but it clicks pretty quickly. And importantly, none of the organizational layers are mandatory. You can ignore the ones that don’t fit your workflow.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Pages&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The highest organizational level is the &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Page&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;When you first open AppTela, it places all your apps on a single page. You can create as many pages as you like.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An app can appear on multiple pages. For example, you might create:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;a &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Side Hustle&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; page&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;a &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;YouTube setup&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; page&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;a &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Daily Work&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; page&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Safari could appear on all of them.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Categories&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Within each page, apps are arranged into &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Categories&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;On the default page, categories appear as headers with apps displayed in a grid beneath them. You can rename, delete, or create categories from the context menu.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The default categories include:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Design and Photography&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Notes&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Entertainment and Media&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Developer Tools&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Education and Reference&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Internet&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Social and Lifestyle&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Utilities&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Video&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;General Applications&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can keep these, modify them, or replace them entirely.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Groups&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you have a lot of apps in a category, &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Groups&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; become useful.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For example, instead of having a giant Utilities grid containing 100 apps, you can break that category into smaller groups.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Here are the &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Utility groups&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; I created:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Automation&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Backup&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Clipboard&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Disk Tools&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Dock Utilities&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;File Maintenance&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;File Transfer&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;File Search&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Hardware&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Maintenance&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Menu Bar&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Network&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Shelf&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Shell&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Shortcuts&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Speech&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;System&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Groups can also be &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;nested up to five levels deep&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;, which gives you a surprising amount of flexibility if you want a very structured layout.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Stacks&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The lowest organizational level is the &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Stack&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There are two kinds.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Regular Stacks&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A regular stack is simply a way to group &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;up to 10 apps&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; inside the space normally occupied by a single icon.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is useful when you have clusters of related tools you only use occasionally.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Launch Stacks&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Launch Stacks look similar, but behave differently.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Clicking one launches &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;every app inside the stack simultaneously&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is perfect for starting a workflow where several tools always open together; for example:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;a writing environment&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;a development setup&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;a media editing session&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Stacks can be placed directly inside a &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;category&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; or inside a &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;group&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Aesthetics and Customization&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;AppTela is extremely customizable.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Almost every visual element can be adjusted; borders, colors, fonts, and backgrounds.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It includes:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;26 display themes&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;29 color schemes&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;7 animated backgrounds&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can run it:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;full screen&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;as a sidebar above the Dock&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;on any display&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;on any Space&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you spend time dialing in a layout you really like, you can &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;lock, save, and back up the configuration&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Wish List&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There are a few things I’d still like to see added.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The biggest one is the ability to launch things other than applications, such as:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Shortcuts&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Folders&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;URLs&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Files&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I would also like something similar to the &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;notes feature in Start (by Innovative Bytes)&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;. Being able to attach a short reference note to an app would be genuinely useful.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Not every app name is descriptive. And if you happen to have &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;six clipboard managers installed&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; (hypothetically speaking), it would be helpful to leave yourself a reminder about which one supports cumulative copying.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;App Details&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Developer Website&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://apptela.com/en/"&gt;AppTela for Mac – Customizable App Launcher &amp;amp; Launchpad Alternative&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Privacy Policy&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;AppTela collects &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;no personal data&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;br&gt;The app runs entirely on your device and requires &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;no network connectivity&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Price&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;$4.99&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; on the &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/apptela-app-launcher/id6752568197?mt=12"&gt;Mac App Store&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Organizing%20a%20660-App%20/Applications%20Folder%20with%20AppTela" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>
    <summary>I recently organized my /Applications folder; it contains more than 660 apps. The tool that finally made it manageable is AppTela, a layered, categorized launcher available for $4.99 on the Mac App Store.

I tend to keep an app for every contingency. The problem isn’t disk space; it’s remembering the name of the utility you...</summary>

    <id>tag:appaddict.app,2005:Post/15943</id>
    <published>2026-04-06T16:26:30Z</published>
    <updated>2026-04-06T16:26:32Z</updated>
    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/i-replaced-apple-music-with-yate-swinsian-navidrome-and-an-ipod-classic-surprisingly-better"/>
    <title>I replaced Apple Music with Yate, Swinsian, Navidrome, and an iPod Classic. Surprisingly better.</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" alt="Navidrome" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBNGlOQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--8be0a070ddcf99c2cafc0fc1df9e97b0cc206ff6/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUNHa0NBQVk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2Q25OMGNtbHdWRG9NY1hWaGJHbDBlV2xrIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--daf4078a1aefa3c961be2c7b8fbe4a74a2641c0c/dylan.jpg" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
    &lt;figcaption class="attachment__caption text-center"&gt;
      Navidrome
    &lt;/figcaption&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;My ten-year experiment with Apple Music is over.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Over the past month I rebuilt my workflow for managing a large local music collection; roughly &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;36,000 tracks&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;. After a lot of experimentation, these are the tools that finally clicked.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Migration&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; – &lt;a href="https://support.apple.com/en-us/108935"&gt;Apple Music with iTunes Match&lt;/a&gt; ($25/year; you only need it once)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Repair&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; – &lt;a href="https://2manyrobots.com/yate/"&gt;Yate&lt;/a&gt; (free)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Management&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; – &lt;a href="https://swinsian.com/"&gt;Swinsian&lt;/a&gt; ($34.95)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Maintenance&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; – Yate + Swinsian&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Consumption (hardware)&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; – &lt;a href="https://www.ebay.com/sch/i.html?_nkw=used+ipod+classic&amp;amp;_sop=12"&gt;iPod Classic&lt;/a&gt; ($40–$400)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Consumption (streaming)&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; – &lt;a href="https://www.navidrome.org/"&gt;Navidrome&lt;/a&gt; (free)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is the story of moving from Apple Music back to &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;files I actually own&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;, and the workflow that makes that practical in 2026.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why Leave?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Streaming trained us to tolerate a mess we never should have accepted.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tracks, albums, and playlists quietly disappear. You’re never quite sure what counts as “your library.” Metadata changes underneath you. And if you cancel the subscription, it’s not always clear what remains.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For casual listening that trade-off may be fine. For anyone who has spent years curating a library, it’s frustrating.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;iPod Enforced Clarity&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Using a big old &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;iPod Classic&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; forces a certain discipline.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Everything must be local.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; No cloud placeholders. Availability becomes certain instead of the streamer’s gamble of “is this still licensed?”&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Metadata has to be correct.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; Artist, Album, Genre, Composer, and Year matter because that’s how the device navigates.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Portability means independence.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; The device doesn’t call home to verify a subscription.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It’s a surprisingly healthy constraint.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;DRM Isn’t What It Used to Be&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;My library comes from a mix of sources:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Ripped CDs&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;iTunes purchases&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Other digital stores (Amazon, eMusic, etc.)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Napster downloads&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In the early years, iTunes purchases were &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;DRM-protected AAC files&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;. Later Apple switched to DRM-free downloads and eventually provided ways to convert older purchases.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That history leaves many long-time iTunes libraries in a messy transitional state.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;iTunes Match Worked for Me&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;$25&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;, iTunes Match will upload up to &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;100,000 songs&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; in almost any format.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The useful trick is what happens next: once the songs are matched or uploaded, you can &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;re-download them as 256 kbps AAC files&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That’s not lossless audiophile territory, but it’s a big improvement over the &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;128 kbps MP3s&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; many of us ripped twenty years ago.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In my case it did two useful things:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Upgraded thousands of low-bitrate files&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Removed DRM from every track I had ever purchased from Apple&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It’s not magic, though.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A “matched” track can sometimes be:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;a different mastering&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;a radio or clean edit&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;a compilation version&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Those substitutions can break album coherence. Keeping a &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;backup of your original files&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; is essential so you can restore anything that gets replaced incorrectly.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" alt="Yate" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBNG1OQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--ac70cdb23c56355b9b96f07593a9a2b1dd78e923/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUNHa0NBQVk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2Q25OMGNtbHdWRG9NY1hWaGJHbDBlV2xrIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--daf4078a1aefa3c961be2c7b8fbe4a74a2641c0c/yate.jpg" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
    &lt;figcaption class="attachment__caption text-center"&gt;
      Yate
    &lt;/figcaption&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Using Yate to Modernize the Library&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Old iTunes libraries accumulate a lot of structural problems.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Artist vs Album Artist inconsistencies&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Compilations explode into dozens of fake albums because Album Artist wasn’t standardized.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Multiple versions of the same artist&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;&lt;code&gt;AC/DC&lt;/code&gt; vs &lt;code&gt;ACDC&lt;/code&gt;, smart quotes, stray spaces, or hidden characters create duplicate artist entries.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Broken multi-disc structure&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Missing disc numbers, merged discs, or tracks numbered 1–12 twice.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Genre chaos&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;&lt;i&gt;&lt;em&gt;Alternative, Alt Rock, Alt. Rock, Indie Rock&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/i&gt; multiplied across 36,000 tracks.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Legacy sorting fields&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Old iTunes “Sort Artist” conventions vary wildly and sometimes actively break browsing.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Artwork inconsistencies&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Some tracks embed artwork, others rely on external caches, and some albums contain multiple covers.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can fix these issues manually for a small collection. Mine required automation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Yate&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; turned out to be the right tool. Its strengths include:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Batch tag repair&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Album Artist normalization, compilation handling, capitalization rules.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Multi-disc metadata fixes&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Correct disc numbers, track numbering, and album naming.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Genre standardization&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Apply a consistent genre system across the library.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Artwork workflows&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Embed artwork consistently and clean up mismatched covers.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Duplicate and anomaly detection&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Surface metadata problems that older iTunes libraries accumulate silently.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" alt="Swinsian" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBNHFOQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--fc4be1e8c6ba7b3a7fa9363832e6820ad83cd056/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUNHa0NBQVk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2Q25OMGNtbHdWRG9NY1hWaGJHbDBlV2xrIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--daf4078a1aefa3c961be2c7b8fbe4a74a2641c0c/CleanShot%202026-04-06%20at%2011.53.10.jpg" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
    &lt;figcaption class="attachment__caption text-center"&gt;
      Swinsian
    &lt;/figcaption&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Swinsian as the Management Layer&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Swinsian is the perfect &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;ongoing management layer&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Yes, it’s a player. But more importantly, it’s a tool for keeping a large collection curated over time.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;What Swinsian Does Well&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;It stays fast.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Even with large libraries. It behaves like a library manager rather than a storefront.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Smart playlists act like real queries.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;You can build them around almost any metadata combination.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Examples from my library:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Tracks added in the last 30 days that are under 256 kbps&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Albums missing artwork&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Tracks with blank Album Artist or “Unknown Album”&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Plays = 0 but rating ≥ 4 stars (a “rediscover” list)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Metadata triage is straightforward.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Sorting by Bit Rate, Kind, Date Added, Album Artist, or Disc Number quickly surfaces problems.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Bulk editing is practical.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Yate handles large automation jobs; Swinsian is perfect for smaller fixes like missing years or Album Artist corrections.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;It’s local-first.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;No cloud substitutions. No licensing surprises. Your library remains exactly what’s on disk.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Files. Tags. Structure.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Drawbacks&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Local libraries come with responsibilities.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Discovery becomes a separate task. There’s no instant “add to playlist” from a streaming catalog.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You also have to care about the plumbing:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;tagging discipline&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;folder structure&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;backups&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;My library uses a simple &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Artist/Album/Track&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; folder structure so both Swinsian and streaming remain predictable.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I’m also paranoid about losing data, so I keep backups on external drives and in the cloud. If you follow a &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;3–2–1 backup strategy&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;, you’re golden. At minimum, use Time Machine.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The upside is control. The downside is maintenance.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What About Streaming?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This turned out to be the easiest part.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Navidrome&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; is the layer that makes your local library available everywhere.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Point it at your curated music folder, let it scan the files, and your collection becomes streamable from:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;phones&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;tablets&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;browsers&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The key advantage is that &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Navidrome reflects your existing organization&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Yate handles tag cleanup and upgrades.&lt;br&gt;Swinsian handles library management and playlists.&lt;br&gt;Navidrome simply serves whatever you’ve already organized.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Once it’s set up, it mostly disappears into the background.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Exactly the way infrastructure should.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;My Current Workflow&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Acquire music (CD rip, digital purchase, download).&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Run Yate actions to normalize tags and artwork.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Import into Swinsian for library management.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Sync to an iPod Classic for offline listening.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Let Navidrome stream the same library remotely.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Closing: The Point Isn’t Nostalgia&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This isn’t a retro flex. It’s an engineering decision.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A locally managed library quietly removes an entire category of annoyances: licensing uncertainty, cloud weirdness, metadata drift, and app strategy whiplash.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;And with the right combination of tools — iTunes Match for upgrades, Yate for tagging, Swinsian for management — a &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;36,000-song library becomes not just manageable, but pleasant again.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=I%20replaced%20Apple%20Music%20with%20Yate,%20Swinsian,%20Navidrome,%20and%20an%20iPod%20Classic.%20Surprisingly%20better." style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>
    <summary>My ten-year experiment with Apple Music is over.

Over the past month I rebuilt my workflow for managing a large local music collection; roughly 36,000 tracks. After a lot of experimentation, these are the tools that finally clicked.

• Migration – Apple Music with iTunes Match ($25/year; you only need it once)
• Repair – Yate (free)...</summary>
